title: Checkout p99 regression traced to an internal load-balancer idle-timeout change (INC-2419)

questions.text: What exactly regressed — which surfaces, by how much, since when, and who is affected?
What caused the checkout tail-latency regression?
Why did alerting, canaries, and SLO machinery miss the regression for 10 days?
Is the fix durable, and what prevents this failure class from recurring?

findings.claim: Checkout (POST /v1/checkout) p99 at weekday peak (14:00-19:00 UTC) has regressed 5.2x, from a 4-week baseline of 310 ms to 1,620 ms, while p50 moved only 58 to 64 ms; the pattern reproduces at every weekday peak since at least Jun 16.

evidence.caption: Checkout p50/p95/p99, 5-min buckets: 4-week baseline overlay vs Jun 16-22, peak window shaded

findings.notes: Anchor finding for the whole pool; p50-flat/p99-blown is the first mechanism constraint.

findings.claim: Checkout edge-timeout errors (504 at the 2,500 ms gateway deadline) run at 0.9% of peak attempts vs 0.05% baseline - an 18x elevation that still sits far below the 5% static error-alert threshold.

evidence.caption: Checkout error rate by hour, Jun 9-22, with gateway 504 breakdown and alert threshold line

findings.claim: Daily-rollup dashboards place the regression onset on Jun 16 afternoon: daily checkout p99 jumps from 470 ms (Jun 15) to 1,540 ms (Jun 16), with the first visibly bad window at ~15:00 UTC.

evidence.caption: Daily p99 rollup, Jun 8-22, with the Jun 15-to-16 step annotated

findings.notes: Deliberately wrong at fine grain: an artifact of the 24h rollup. Overturned by F20; the misread anchors the pricing hypothesis (F05).

findings.claim: The regression is confined to the two ledger-backed endpoints - checkout p99 310 to 1,620 ms and order-status p99 120 to 1,560 ms - while browse (145 ms) and cart (210 ms) p99s are unchanged, implicating the orders-to-ledger path rather than the edge or shared middleware.

evidence.caption: Per-endpoint p99, baseline vs Jun 16-22 peak, grouped by backing data store

findings.claim: pricing-svc v341 (deployed Jun 16 14:20 UTC, new rules engine) is the leading suspect: it is the only order-path change in the deploy tracker near the apparent Jun 16 onset, and pricing's own peak p99 rose from 45 to 85 ms the same day.

evidence.caption: Deploy-tracker entries Jun 14-17 vs pricing-svc p99, with v341 deploy marker

findings.notes: The red herring. The +40 ms is real (rules-engine cost) but benign for checkout (parallel call). Overturned by F16.

findings.claim: The edge-log latency histogram at peak is bimodal: 4.3% of checkout attempts either exceed 1.5 s (3.4%, clustered at 1.56-1.75 s) or return 504 (0.9%); off-peak the combined share is under 0.3%. Impact is peak-concentrated and quantized, not a uniform slowdown.

evidence.caption: Checkout latency histogram from edge logs, peak vs off-peak, log-scale x, 504s as terminal bar

findings.notes: The 4.3% here must reconcile with F21's 4.2% exposure (rounding seam is deliberate and documented in DESIGN 5.3).

findings.claim: Distributed-trace aggregation over the Jun 16-22 peaks puts the entire p99 excess in the orders-api ledger-transaction phase (span p99 +1,510 ms vs baseline); pricing (+40 ms) and inventory (+2 ms) span deltas cannot account for the checkout regression.

evidence.caption: Span-level p99 deltas by service phase, checkout traces, baseline vs regressed peaks

findings.notes: Already in tension with F05; the team rationalized it ('v341 changes the write mix') - true-to-life cognitive inertia.

findings.claim: The ledger Postgres primary is healthy throughout the regression: server-side query p99 is 11 ms (unchanged), zero lock waits over 100 ms, CPU 38%, buffer-cache hit 99.2% - the excess latency accrues between orders-api and the database, not inside it.

evidence.caption: Ledger primary server metrics, Jun 9-22: query p99, locks, CPU, cache hit ratio

findings.claim: The 02:00-03:10 UTC analytics batch evicts 91% of the ledger primary's buffer cache nightly; first-morning queries pay +35 ms for roughly 20 minutes after traffic resumes. Wrong hours and wrong magnitude for the peak regression, but worth a capacity ticket.

evidence.caption: Buffer-cache hit ratio and first-query latency around the nightly analytics window

findings.notes: Tangential drive-by found while inspecting DB dashboards; bears on no open question - routing stress.

findings.claim: Rolling pricing back to v340 at Jun 24 11:30 - bundled with a precautionary orders-api rolling restart - dropped checkout p99 from 1,590 to 348 ms within 10 minutes, read at the time as confirmation of the pricing hypothesis.

evidence.caption: Checkout p99 around the Jun 24 11:30 intervention (pricing rollback + orders-api restart)

values.intervention: pricing v340 rollback + orders-api rolling restart

findings.notes: Confounded two-change intervention - the classic false fix. Overturned by F15.

findings.claim: The regression returned the same day despite the rollback: the Jun 24 peak reached p99 1,610 ms by 15:05 with pricing still on v340 - so either checkout regressed again independently, or the pricing hypothesis is wrong.

evidence.caption: Checkout p99, Jun 24 full day: 11:30 intervention, ~40-min recovery, relapse into the peak

findings.claim: A sweep of the deploy tracker for Jun 12-16 finds no order-path application deploys other than pricing v341; however the tracker does not ingest infrastructure or network changes, so the sweep cannot exclude infra causes.

evidence.caption: Deploy-tracker query results, Jun 12-16, order-path services, with coverage caveat

findings.notes: The coverage caveat is the seed of F32 (change-visibility gap) once Q3 exists.

findings.claim: orders-api's container image is 1.34 GB, of which a stale 480 MB debug layer (leftover profiler bundle) is never used; it adds ~90 s of pull time per pod and stretched the 12-pod rolling restart to 19 minutes versus ~9 without it.

evidence.caption: Image layer inventory for orders-api:current with per-layer pull timings

findings.notes: Tangential drive-by noticed while watching the Jun 24 rolling restart; bears on no question.

findings.claim: With checkout tracing raised to 100% (Jun 25 09:20), every slow exemplar contains exactly one ledger span of 1,500 +/- 8 ms - the configured pgJDBC socketTimeout - followed by a 21 ms retry (12 ms connection setup + 9 ms query). The excess is a single quantized read-timeout, not gradual slowness.

evidence.caption: Trace-exemplar extraction over 214 slow checkouts: span duration histogram peaks at socketTimeout

findings.notes: Pivotal mechanism clue: the fixed 1,521 ms penalty every dependent number rests on.

findings.claim: Across all three orders-api restart events (Jun 19 03:10 routine deploy, Jun 24 11:30 rollback bundle, Jun 25 09:45 manual), checkout p99 recovers to ~350 ms and relapses within 38-44 minutes, independent of pricing version - the Jun 24 'fix' was the restart, not the rollback.

evidence.caption: Checkout p99 overlaid and time-aligned on three orders-api restart events, pricing version annotated per event

findings.notes: First overturn (position 15/40): kills the false-fix reading with the Jun 19 event as a natural control.

findings.claim: Re-deploying pricing v341 to a 10% canary cell (Jun 25 16:00) with no orders-api restart leaves checkout p99 unchanged - 1,615 ms in-cell vs 1,625 ms control across the 16:00-19:00 peak - exonerating pricing v341 as the cause of the checkout regression.

evidence.caption: Controlled canary: checkout p99, v341 cell vs v340 control, Jun 25 peak window

findings.notes: Second overturn (16/40): the controlled experiment the Jun 24 intervention should have been.

findings.claim: In 9 of 9 hand-dissected slow exemplars, the 1,500 ms span is the first use of its pooled connection after an idle period of at least 60 s (range 61-214 s); no exemplar shows a timeout on a recently-used connection - consistent with idle connections dying silently.

evidence.caption: Per-exemplar connection idle-time-before-failure, joined from pool logs and trace ids

findings.notes: Small n, manual join - weak on purpose; F22 later confirms at counter scale.

findings.claim: Business impact corroborates the ops signal: checkout conversion fell 1.8% week-over-week for Jun 16-22, and 'slow checkout' support tickets rose to 212 versus 31 in the baseline week.

evidence.caption: Weekly conversion funnel and tagged support-ticket counts, Jun 9-15 vs Jun 16-22

findings.notes: Correlational business data; also the path by which the incident was actually noticed (weekly review, partner escalation).

findings.claim: tcpdump on a production orders-api pod shows connections idle >= 60 s are silently blackholed: the first packet after idle is retransmitted 3 times with exponential backoff and never answered - no RST, no FIN - until the 1,500 ms read deadline; connections idle under 58 s behave normally.

evidence.caption: Packet capture, orders-api pod to ledger VIP, Jun 26 14:50-16:10 UTC, annotated retransmit sequences

findings.notes: Direct mechanism observation; the no-RST detail is what makes the failure silent to the client stack.

findings.claim: A 5-min per-AZ percentile reconstruction from edge logs moves the true onset to Jun 12 22:10 UTC in AZ-a alone (AZ-a p99 ~1,600 ms while fleet p99 read 480 ms on Jun 15) with a second, fleet-wide step at Jun 16 11:33 in AZ-b/c - four days before, and three hours before, the pricing deploy respectively. The 'Jun 16 onset' was a rollup artifact.

evidence.caption: Per-AZ checkout p99 at 5-min grain, Jun 11-17, with both steps and the pricing deploy marker

findings.notes: Third overturn (20/40). The 20/40/40 AZ split (May 21 drain) is why stage 1 stayed sub-threshold at fleet grain.

findings.claim: The new ledger.pool.dead_on_borrow counter (deployed Jun 26 13:00) reads 19.7/s fleet-wide at peak - 13.0/s on the checkout path and 6.7/s on order-status - i.e. 1.4% of 1,410 borrows/s; at 3 borrows per checkout that is 4.2% of checkouts exposed, matching the 4.3% slow-or-error share in the edge histogram within rounding.

evidence.caption: dead_on_borrow rate by endpoint path, Jun 26 peak, vs borrow volume and per-request exposure arithmetic

findings.notes: Quantifies both impact (Q1) and mechanism (Q2); the arithmetic seam with F06 is documented in DESIGN 5.2-5.3.

findings.claim: Splitting dead borrows by connection idle age: 100% occur on connections idle >= 60 s (median 96 s at death) and zero on connections idle <= 58 s - a hard threshold at ~60 s of idle, pointing at a fixed idle-timeout somewhere on the connection path.

evidence.caption: Dead-borrow probability vs connection idle age, 2-s buckets, Jun 26-27 peaks

findings.notes: The 60 s threshold becomes the search key that finds NETOPS-4112 (F24).

findings.claim: Pool telemetry explains both the peak-only symptom and the ~40-min post-restart relapse: peak bursts swell each pod's pool from 55 to 85 connections and lulls idle them past 60 s - the 60-600 s idle 'landmine' cohort averages 11% of the pool at peak versus under 1% off-peak, and takes about 40 minutes to first form after a restart.

evidence.caption: Per-pod open connections and landmine-cohort share over a peak day, with post-restart formation time

findings.notes: Closes the loop on F15's 38-44 min relapse window and on why off-peak is clean (small hot pools).

findings.claim: Change record NETOPS-4112 lowered the internal L4 load-balancer idle-flow timeout from 350 s to 60 s (connection-table hardening after the May 30 exhaustion incident; occupancy target 2.1M to 640k entries), staged AZ-a Jun 12 22:04 and AZ-b/c Jun 16 11:30 - matching the 60 s death threshold and both onset steps; the ilb's eviction policy drops non-SYN packets of evicted flows without RST.

evidence.caption: NETOPS-4112 change record and ilb config diff, with staged rollout timestamps and eviction-policy excerpt

findings.notes: Root cause identified. Found only after F22's 60 s key + F20's timing made the netops system worth searching (F32 tells that story for Q3).

findings.claim: Per-AZ latency step times match the staged NETOPS-4112 rollout to within minutes: AZ-a config 22:04 vs step 22:10; AZ-b/c config 11:30 vs step 11:33 - a 3-6 minute lag consistent with the first post-change 60 s idle windows elapsing.

evidence.caption: Config-push timestamps vs first elevated 5-min bucket, per AZ

findings.claim: Staging reproduction: behind an ilb configured with a 60 s idle timeout, a pooled connection idled 65 s blackholes on next use - 3 unanswered retransmits, a 1,500 ms read timeout, then a 21 ms reconnect-and-retry - matching the production exemplar signature exactly; with the timeout at 350 s the same procedure is clean.

evidence.caption: Staging repro harness output: idle-then-use at 65 s under 60 s vs 350 s ilb idle timeout

findings.notes: Koch-postulate step: cause reproduced and toggled off in isolation.

findings.claim: Order-status corroborates the per-borrow arithmetic: with 1 ledger borrow per request (vs checkout's 3), 1.4% of status requests burn (vs 4.2%), and both endpoints' regressed p99s converge just above the fixed penalty - 1,560 ms (baseline 120) and 1,620 ms (baseline 310) - the signature of a single constant 1,521 ms fault rather than load-dependent slowness.

evidence.caption: Checkout vs order-status: borrows per request, burn fraction, baseline and regressed p99

findings.notes: Cross-endpoint consistency check; the quantile arithmetic is in DESIGN 5.4.

findings.claim: Reverting the ilb idle timeout to 350 s in AZ-b only (Jun 27 18:40) drops AZ-b dead borrows from 7.9 to 0.1/s within 12 minutes and AZ-b checkout p99 from 1,610 to 335 ms by 19:10, while AZ-a/c controls are unchanged (~1,620 ms) - causal confirmation and the first fix validation in one experiment.

evidence.caption: Dead-borrow rate and checkout p99 per AZ around the Jun 27 18:40 AZ-b revert

findings.notes: First Q4 evidence (position 28/40) - the proactive-intent gap closes here. AZ-b carries 40% of traffic: 19.7 x 0.4 = 7.9/s.

findings.claim: The checkout p99 page threshold had been raised from 800 to 2,500 ms on Mar 11 2026 (OBS-1873, 'flapping during spring sale') with an unactioned revert TODO; all five regressed weekday peaks (1,590-1,655 ms) sat under the raised threshold - the original 800 ms threshold would have paged on Jun 16.

evidence.caption: Alert-config change history for checkout p99, with regressed peak values plotted against both thresholds

findings.notes: First Q3 finding (position 29/40) - the emergent question opens here.

findings.claim: SLO math shows the miss was procedural, not informational: daily error-budget burn ran 4.4x from Jun 16 (peak-hour burn 9x vs the 14.4x fast-burn page threshold), the 3x slow-burn rule filed 23 tickets into an untriaged queue, and June's checkout budget was 100% consumed by Jun 22 20:00 - before the incident was even opened.

evidence.caption: Burn-rate reconstruction Jun 12-23: hourly and daily burn vs page/ticket thresholds, budget depletion curve

findings.notes: Burn arithmetic derives from F02's error rates; see DESIGN 5.6.

findings.claim: The synthetic canary was blind by construction: one probe per minute at concurrency 1 from 2 regions, each probe on a fresh connection - it can never borrow a pooled connection that has idled past 60 s, and canary p99 read 313-317 ms through the entire incident.

evidence.caption: Canary probe design parameters vs the failure preconditions, with canary p99 series Jun 12-27

findings.notes: Explains blindness via the mechanism's preconditions (needs F22's idle threshold); F40 later fixes it.

findings.claim: Root-cause attribution lost roughly 3 days to a change-visibility gap: triage consulted only the deploy tracker, which does not ingest netops changes; NETOPS-4112 sat in a separate system and was found only once the 60 s idle threshold provided a targeted search key.

evidence.caption: Timeline of change-source consultation during INC-2419, with tracker coverage matrix

findings.claim: The Jun-16 onset misread traces to the ops dashboard's default 24 h rollup grain: the 5-min percentile store held the Jun-12 AZ-a step all along, but the default view collapsed it - and the misread anchored the pricing hypothesis for two days.

evidence.caption: Same underlying series rendered at 24 h vs 5-min grain, side by side, with the Jun 12 step visible only at 5-min

findings.notes: Interpretive attribution linking F03's error to a tooling default; bridges Q1's history to Q3's lesson.

findings.claim: On-call context evaporated across three handoffs (Jun 15-22): each shift logged the elevated peaks as 'high but in-SLO, likely summer promo' and no shift compared against the prior week - the runbook contains no cross-shift trend review step.

evidence.caption: Shift-log excerpts and handoff notes, Jun 15-22, coded for how each shift explained the elevated peaks

findings.notes: Anecdotal shift-log review; independent of the technical chain, discoverable any time after the incident opens.

findings.claim: The fleet-wide revert to 350 s plus client hardening (TCP keepalive 30 s via pod sysctl, HikariCP keepaliveTime 30 s, idleTimeout 600 to 45 s) shipped Jun 28 09:00; the Jun 29 peak was clean: p99 318 ms, errors 0.05%, dead borrows 0.0/s.

evidence.caption: Post-fix Jun 29 peak scorecard vs baseline: p99, error rate, dead-borrow counter

findings.notes: Defense in depth: even if an LB timeout drops again, client keepalive (30 s) and eviction (45 s) stay under any plausible floor.

findings.claim: inventory-svc emits 4.3k WARN lines/min (38% of its log volume) for the deprecated warehouse_zone field - pure noise that measurably slowed log searches during the investigation; filed as a hygiene ticket.

evidence.caption: Log-volume breakdown for inventory-svc by level and message template, Jun 23-27

findings.notes: Tangential drive-by from log sweeps; bears on no question - routing stress.

findings.claim: Replaying the restored alert policy (800 ms p99 threshold plus the 14.4x/3x multiwindow burn rules) against June telemetry first pages at Jun 16 12:07 - 6.9 days before the actual Jun 23 10:15 detection; the stage-1 AZ-a period (fleet p99 480 ms) is still missed by every threshold rule, leaving the pooled-canary class (F40) as the only cover for it.

evidence.caption: Alert-replay harness over Jun 12-23 telemetry: first-page times under old, raised, and restored policies

findings.notes: Honest negative half: threshold restoration alone does not cover single-AZ partial failures.

findings.claim: A 2x-peak load test (620 rps checkout, Jul 2) on the hardened configuration holds p50 59 ms / p99 322 ms with zero dead borrows and the same 55-85 per-pod pool oscillation - the fix is not load-marginal.

evidence.caption: Load-test report: latency percentiles, dead-borrow counter, and pool telemetry at 620 rps sustained 2 h

findings.claim: A conformance sweep of all 41 service-to-dependency pairs (client keepalive/idle-eviction vs path idle timeout) found 3 more latent pairs with the same failure geometry: notifications to queue-broker (keepalive off, eviction 900 s), exports to object-gateway (keepalive 300 s vs LB 120 s), and search-indexer to ledger-replica (keepalive off, eviction 600 s).

evidence.caption: Keepalive/eviction vs path-timeout matrix for 41 service pairs, violations highlighted

findings.notes: Generalizes the root cause into a failure class (Q2 blast radius) and a standing guardrail (Q4).

findings.claim: A redesigned canary holding a persistent connection pool with forced 90 s idle cycles detects this failure class directly: in a staging game-day that re-lowered the ilb timeout to 60 s, the canary alarmed in 9 minutes - versus 10.5 days for the June incident.

evidence.caption: Game-day log: staged ilb timeout drop vs pooled-canary alarm timeline

findings.notes: Closes both Q3 (the blindness is fixed) and Q4 (the class is detectable), including the stage-1 gap F37 left open.
